title: Life Together: Humility, Care, and Forgiveness
summary: When the disciples ask who is greatest, Jesus sets a child among them and teaches humility, warns severely against causing little ones to stumble, and tells of a shepherd who searches for one straying sheep. He gives steps for dealing with a brother who sins, promising his presence where two or three gather in his name. To Peter's question about how often to forgive, he answers seventy-seven times and tells the parable of a servant forgiven a vast debt who refuses to forgive a small one.
story:
Having taught his disciples twice that he must suffer (16:21; 17:22-23), Jesus now teaches them how to live together as his community. This is the fourth of Matthew's five great discourses, often called the community discourse, and like the others it ends with the formula ‘When Jesus had finished saying these things’ (19:1). It follows the promise that Jesus will build his church (16:18), and it is the only other place in the Gospels where the word church appears (verse 17). The setting in Capernaum is private: the audience is the disciples, not the crowds, and the question that starts it is theirs.

The chapter moves from status to care to discipline to forgiveness, and each section corrects a natural instinct. The disciples ask about greatness; Jesus answers with a child. They might despise the weak; he warns of a millstone. They might let a straying member go; he tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine to search. They might tolerate sin or gossip about it; he tells them to go privately to the brother. Peter might count how often to forgive; Jesus answers with a debt no one could repay. The previous chapter ended with Jesus paying a tax he did not owe ‘so that we may not offend them’, and this chapter takes up the same concern for not causing others to stumble as the first mark of his people.
historical:
The chapter's instructions for dealing with sin draw on the law of Moses. Deuteronomy 19:15 required two or three witnesses to establish a charge, and verse 16 quotes it in a shortened form; Leviticus 19:17-18 commands Israel, “Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him,” and forbids revenge or a grudge. Jewish communities of the period built procedures on these texts. The Community Rule from Qumran requires a member to reprove his fellow in truth and humility and forbids bringing a matter before the assembly (the Many) without first reproving him before witnesses (1QS 5:24-6:1), and the Damascus Document says that anyone who brings a charge against his fellow without first reproving him before witnesses is taking vengeance, in breach of Leviticus 19:18 (CD 9:2-8). The Testament of Gad, one of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs (a collection whose date and Jewish or Christian origin are debated), urges the reader to speak peaceably to one who sins against him and, if he repents and confesses, to forgive him (Testament of Gad 6:3-7). Jewish teachers also discussed the limits of forgiveness: a saying of Rabbi Yose bar Judah in the Babylonian Talmud holds that a person who sins is forgiven a first, second, and third time but not a fourth (b. Yoma 86b), and the Mishnah teaches that the Day of Atonement does not atone for wrongs done to another person until the wrongdoer has appeased him (m. Yoma 8:9).

The parable's sums would have stunned its hearers. The talent was originally a weight of silver, somewhere between about 26 and 34 kilograms depending on the standard, and as money it was worth about six thousand drachmas or denarii; a denarius was a laborer's day wage (20:2). Ten thousand talents, sixty million denarii, joins the largest Greek number word (myrias, ten thousand) to the largest unit of money; a laborer would need something like two hundred thousand years to earn it. Josephus says the annual revenue assigned to Herod Antipas from Galilee and Perea was two hundred talents, to Philip one hundred, and to Archelaus six hundred (Antiquities 17.318-320), and he reckons that after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC the Romans exacted more than ten thousand talents from the Jews in a short time (Antiquities 14.78). Haman's bribe to destroy the Jews in Esther 3:9 is the same sum. The fellow servant's hundred denarii, about a hundred days' wages, was real money, but the ratio between the two debts is six hundred thousand to one.

The king's orders reflect the harsher practice of Gentile courts more than Jewish law. Israel knew debt slavery (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:5), but the law limited it (Leviticus 25:39-43; Deuteronomy 15:12-15), and the Mishnah rules that a man may be sold for his theft but a woman may not (m. Sotah 3:8, on Exodus 22:3). Imprisonment until a debt was paid and the handing of a debtor to torturers (basanistai, verse 34) belong to the Hellenistic and Roman world, and Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus) observed that these details point to a non-Jewish royal court. Jesus' hearers would have pictured a great king and his high officials, men who farmed the revenues of whole provinces. The parallels to the rest of the chapter are Mark 9:33-50 and Luke 9:46-48 for greatness and stumbling, Luke 15:3-7 for the lost sheep, and Luke 17:1-4 for rebuke and forgiveness.
cultural:
Children in the ancient world were loved but had little standing. They were legal minors under their father's authority, valued chiefly for what they would become, and Greek could use the same word, pais, for a child and a slave. To ‘change and become like little children’ (verse 3; the verb strephō means to turn) is not to become innocent or naive but to give up the contest for rank and to depend on another. Welcoming a child in Jesus' name (verse 5) means receiving the least as one would receive him, a principle of agency found in the Mishnah's saying that a man's agent is as the man himself (m. Berakhot 5:5). The ‘little ones who believe in Me’ (verse 6) are not only children but vulnerable disciples, as in 10:42, where a cup of water is given to ‘one of these little ones because he is My disciple’.

The millstone in verse 6 is literally a donkey's millstone (mylos onikos), the large upper stone of a mill turned by an animal, far heavier than the hand mill of a household. Drowning with a weight tied to the neck was a known punishment: Suetonius says Augustus had the tutor and servants of his adopted son Gaius thrown into a river with heavy weights around their necks for abusing their positions (Augustus 67). The warnings of verses 8 and 9 repeat 5:29-30 in a new setting, and their hyperbole, cutting off a hand or tearing out an eye, is a vivid way of saying that nothing is worth keeping if it leads to ruin; the church has never read them as a command to harm the body. Hell in verse 9 is Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once the site of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), which became a name for the place of final judgment.

Jewish belief in angels assigned to people and nations stands behind verse 10. The angel Raphael accompanies Tobias and calls himself one of the seven angels who stand ready and enter before the glory of the Lord (Tobit 12:15); Psalm 91:11 speaks of angels charged to guard God's people; and in Acts 12:15 the believers, hearing Peter at the door, say it must be his angel. To ‘see the face’ of a king meant to have access to his presence, so the little ones' angels have the Father's ear. Shepherds counted their flocks each evening, and a hundred sheep was a modest flock; the phrase ‘on the hills’ echoes Ezekiel 34:6, where God's sheep went astray ‘on all the mountains and every high hill’. Tax collectors and pagans (Gentiles) in verse 17 were the stock figures for those outside Israel's community, though Matthew's readers knew that Jesus ate with tax collectors (9:10-11; 11:19) and that the Gospel's namesake had been one (9:9). The rabbis said that the divine presence rests among ten who study the law together, and even among two, and even with one (m. Avot 3:2, 3:6); a quorum of ten was needed for public prayer (m. Megillah 4:3). Jesus' ‘two or three gathered in My name’ speaks the same language and places himself where the rabbis placed the Presence.
literary:
The discourse has two halves, each opened by a question (verses 1 and 21). The first half concerns the little ones: humility (verses 1 to 5), not causing them to stumble (verses 6 to 9), and seeking them when they stray (verses 10 to 14); it is held together by the phrase ‘these little ones’ in verses 6, 10, and 14. The second half concerns the brother who sins: correction (verses 15 to 20) and forgiveness (verses 21 to 35), held together by the word brother (verses 15, 21, and 35). Each half ends with a word about the Father in heaven: he is not willing that any little one should perish (verse 14), and he will treat the unforgiving as the king did (verse 35). The two halves balance each other. The community must seek those who wander and confront those who sin, but it must always forgive.

Matthew has reshaped material found scattered in Mark and Luke into one address to the church. Mark says the disciples argued on the road about who was greatest and fell silent when asked (Mark 9:33-34); Matthew has them ask Jesus outright. Luke tells the lost sheep in answer to Pharisees who grumbled that Jesus received sinners (Luke 15:1-7), and there the sheep is ‘lost’ and the shepherd searches ‘until he finds it’; Matthew addresses the disciples, speaks of a sheep that ‘goes astray’ (planaō, a word used for being led into error, 24:4-5), and says ‘if he finds it’, so the parable becomes a charge to pastors and members not to let a wandering believer go. Luke's version ends with joy in heaven over one sinner who repents; Matthew's with the Father's will that none of the little ones perish.

The parable of the unforgiving servant (verses 23 to 35) is built in three scenes, each with a plea and a response. In the first the servant falls on his knees and says, ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay back everything’, and the master, moved with compassion, forgives the whole debt. In the second the fellow servant falls down and says almost the same words, ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay you back’, and the forgiven servant has him thrown into prison. In the third the master summons him and turns his own words against him. The near repetition of the plea in verses 26 and 29 is the hinge: the reader hears the servant's own request in another's mouth and waits to see whether he will recognize it. The debt language ties the parable to the Lord's Prayer, “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (6:12), and to Jesus' comment on it (6:14-15). Verse 11, found in later manuscripts, repeats Luke 19:10 (see the note on the text).

outline.t: The greatest in the kingdom: become like a child
Warnings against causing others to stumble
The straying sheep and the Father's will
When a brother sins: correction and restoration
How often to forgive: the unforgiving servant

doctrines.note: This is Jesus' instruction for his community, and the second of only two uses of the word church in the Gospels (verse 17). It is marked by humility rather than rank, protective care for the vulnerable, patient correction aimed at winning the brother back, authority to bind and loose given to the gathered community (verse 18), and the presence of Jesus himself where two or three gather in his name (verse 20).

Verse 10 says that the little ones' angels in heaven always see the Father's face. The verse became the main text for the church's teaching that God assigns angels to guard his people (Jerome, Aquinas), though Christians differ over how far it teaches an angel for each person. Its point in context is the worth of the least disciple: they have access to the Father's presence, so no one may despise them.

The chapter takes sin seriously in every direction: causing a vulnerable believer to fall brings a fearful woe (verses 6 and 7), one's own sin must be cut away at any cost (verses 8 and 9), and a brother's sin must be faced rather than ignored (verse 15). Yet the aim in dealing with sin is always restoration: ‘you have won your brother over’.

The forgiven debt in the parable pictures God's mercy: a debt no one could ever repay, cancelled by a king who ‘had compassion on him’ (verse 27). That mercy is meant to remake the one who receives it, so that the forgiven forgive ‘from your heart’ (verse 35).

The chapter ends with a warning: the Father will treat the unforgiving as the master treated the servant who would not show mercy (verse 35), and verses 8 and 9 speak of eternal fire and the fire of hell. Judgment here is not a threat to outsiders but a warning to disciples that mercy refused reveals a heart that has not received mercy.

words.note: Paidion, little child, the diminutive of pais; about fifty-two times in the New Testament, eighteen in Matthew. It can mean an infant (2:8-9, of the child Jesus) or a young child old enough to stand among the disciples, as here (verse 2). Jesus calls the one who humbles himself (tapeinoō) like this child the greatest in the kingdom (verse 4); Matthew uses the adjective from the same family of Jesus himself, ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29). The greatest in the kingdom resemble the king.

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to trip up, to lead into sin; about twenty-nine times in the New Testament, fourteen in Matthew, three in verses 6 to 9, with the noun skandalon three times in verse 7. The picture is of a trap or an obstacle in the road. In verse 6 it means leading a believer away from faith; in verses 8 and 9 it means whatever in one's own life causes one to fall. The chapter's concern is not minor offense but ruin, especially of someone vulnerable.

Planaō, to lead astray, and in the passive to wander or go astray; about thirty-nine times in the New Testament, eight in Matthew, four in verses 12 and 13. Elsewhere in Matthew it describes being deceived by false teaching (22:29) and by false messiahs (24:4-5, 11, 24). Matthew's shepherd seeks a sheep that has wandered, a believer in danger of being lost through error or neglect, which is why the parable stands among instructions to the church.

Elegchō, to bring to light, expose, convict, or correct; about eighteen times in the New Testament, only here in Matthew (verse 15, BSB ‘confront him privately’). It is the verb of the Greek Old Testament in Leviticus 19:17, the command to rebuke one's neighbor. BDAG gives senses ranging from exposing a fault to convincing someone of it. The goal in verse 15 is not humiliation but a hearing: ‘If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.’

Aphiēmi, to let go, release, leave, permit, and so to forgive; with its related senses about 146 times in the New Testament, forty-seven in Matthew. It is the ordinary word for cancelling a debt, and the king ‘forgave his debt’ (verse 27; ‘I forgave all your debt’, verse 32) in the same sense. The Lord's Prayer uses it of debts (6:12), and Jesus uses it at the Last Supper, where his blood is poured out ‘for the forgiveness of sins’ (26:28, the noun aphesis). Forgiveness in this chapter is release of a real debt, not denial that it exists.

Hebdomēkontakis, seventy times; only here in the New Testament. Jesus answers ‘not seven times, but hebdomēkontakis hepta’, which can mean seventy-seven times or seventy times seven. The Greek Old Testament of Genesis 4:24 uses the same phrase for Lamech's boast that he would be avenged seventy-sevenfold, where the Hebrew clearly means seventy-seven, and most modern versions follow that sense; older ones read seventy times seven. Either way, forgiveness is not to be counted, and Lamech's unlimited revenge is answered by unlimited forgiveness.

Talanton, talent; fourteen times in the New Testament, all in Matthew (here and in the parable of the talents, 25:14-30). Originally a weight, it became the largest unit of money, worth about six thousand denarii. Ten thousand talents is a figure meant to be beyond calculation, like the debt of sin before God. The English sense of talent as natural ability comes from later readings of Matthew 25, not from this word.

Splanchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inward parts thought of as the seat of feeling; twelve times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels, five of them in Matthew. Outside the parables it is used only of Jesus, who has compassion on the crowds (9:36; 14:14; 15:32) and on two blind men (20:34). When the master is ‘moved with compassion’ (verse 27), the parable's king acts as Jesus does.

christ:
Jesus speaks here as the Lord of his church. The promise that where two or three gather in his name ‘there am I with them’ (verse 20) takes the language Jewish teachers used of the divine presence resting among those who study the law together (m. Avot 3:2, 3:6) and applies it to himself. It stands between the two great promises that frame Matthew's Gospel: that his name is Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23), and that he will be with his disciples always, to the end of the age (28:20). Only one who is God with us could make such a promise.

The parable of the straying sheep reflects Ezekiel 34, where God, rebuking Israel's shepherds for leaving the flock scattered, promises, “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16). Matthew has already said that Jesus had compassion on the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd (9:36) and that he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel (15:24); in his passion he will be the shepherd struck so that the sheep scatter (26:31, quoting Zechariah 13:7). The Father's unwillingness that any little one perish is what Jesus himself enacts. The link to Ezekiel is thematic rather than a quoted fulfillment, but it is strong.

The parable of the unforgiving servant pictures the grace Jesus brings. The king's cancellation of an unpayable debt anticipates the cross, where Jesus gives his blood ‘for the forgiveness of sins’ (26:28), and the king's compassion (splanchnizomai) is the compassion Matthew attributes to Jesus himself. Jesus is also the model of the humility he commends: the Son who is ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29) and who came ‘not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many’ (20:28). The greatest in the kingdom is the one who took the lowest place, and the church he gathers is to bear his likeness.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition developed its own teaching on correction and forgiveness from the same texts. The Mishnah's rule that the Day of Atonement does not atone for wrongs against another until he is appeased (m. Yoma 8:9) shaped the custom of seeking forgiveness from those one has wronged in the days before Yom Kippur. Maimonides (Laws of Repentance 2:9-10, in the Mishneh Torah, twelfth century) taught that the wrongdoer must ask forgiveness, returning up to three times with others if refused, and that the one wronged should not be cruel and refuse to be appeased but should forgive wholeheartedly when asked. The Talmudic limit of three times (b. Yoma 86b) is often set beside Peter's offer of seven.

In the church, verse 10 became the classic text for guardian angels. Jerome, in his Commentary on Matthew (398), wrote that the dignity of souls is great, since each has an angel appointed to guard it from birth, and Thomas Aquinas cited the verse in his treatment of the guardianship of angels (Summa Theologiae I.113). Pope Clement X made the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2 universal in 1670, and its Gospel is taken from this chapter. The procedure of verses 15 to 17 shaped monastic life: the Rule of Benedict (chapter 23, sixth century) directs that a brother at fault be admonished privately a first and second time, as the Lord commanded, before public rebuke or exclusion. In the sixteenth century the chapter was at the center of arguments over discipline. The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527, article 2) required that a member who fell into sin be admonished twice privately and the third time publicly, before the breaking of bread. Luther's treatise The Keys (1530) read verse 18 as giving the keys to the whole church. John Calvin gave a chapter of the Institutes (4.12) to church discipline, and the Belgic Confession (1561, article 29) named discipline as one of the marks of a true church. The Heidelberg physician Thomas Erastus argued that excommunication had no warrant in Scripture and that punishing sin belonged to the Christian magistrate; his treatise was published after his death in 1589, and Theodore Beza replied in 1590. The debate gave English the word Erastian.

The parable of the unforgiving servant has been read through the Lord's Prayer since the fathers. Luther's Large Catechism (1529), explaining the fifth petition, called the clause ‘as we forgive’ a necessary and comforting addition: God has promised that we may be sure we are forgiven, and our forgiving others is a sign he attached to the promise. In the twentieth century Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Life Together (1939), written from the seminary community at Finkenwalde, made mutual correction, confession, and forgiveness the marks of Christian community, and theologians such as L. Gregory Jones (Embodying Forgiveness, 1995) and Miroslav Volf (Exclusion and Embrace, 1996) set the parable in conversation with the problem of forgiveness after atrocity. Simon Wiesenthal's The Sunflower (1969, English 1970), in which a dying SS soldier asks a Jewish prisoner to forgive him, gathered Jewish and Christian responses that show how differently the traditions answer whether one may forgive on behalf of others.

In worship, the Revised Common Lectionary reads Matthew 18:15-20 and 18:21-35 on Propers 18 and 19 in Year A, and the Roman lectionary on the Twenty-Third and Twenty-Fourth Sundays in Ordinary Time in Year A. The image of the shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders is among the oldest Christian pictures, found on the walls of the Roman catacombs and in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria (about 240s). Elizabeth Clephane's poem ‘The Ninety and Nine’ (1868), set to music by Ira Sankey in 1874, carried the parable into the gospel song tradition.
text:
Verse 11, ‘For the Son of Man came to save the lost’, is missing from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and other early witnesses of several text types. It appears in most later manuscripts and in the King James Version, and editors judge that it was borrowed from Luke 19:10, perhaps to link verse 10 to the parable that follows. The BSB leaves the verse number empty, so the numbering skips from 10 to 12.

In verse 15 the words ‘against you’ (eis se) are absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and present in most other manuscripts. The Nestle-Aland text prints them in brackets. Translations divide: the BSB, ESV, and NRSV keep ‘sins against you’, while the current NIV and the NET read simply ‘if your brother or sister sins’. The difference matters for application. With the words, the passage is about a personal offense between two believers; without them, it becomes a broader duty to correct any brother's sin. Some scholars think the words were added from verse 21; others think they dropped out by accident, since they sound almost like the ending of the verb before them.

In verse 14 manuscripts differ between ‘your Father’ and ‘my Father’. In verse 22 the Greek hebdomēkontakis hepta is translated ‘seventy times seven’ in the King James Version and the RSV, and ‘seventy-seven times’ in the BSB, NIV, ESV, and NRSV, usually with the other rendering in a note (see the word note above). In verse 35 later manuscripts add ‘their trespasses’ at the end, which the King James Version translates.

teach.big: Jesus' community is marked by the humility of children, fierce protection of the vulnerable, persistent pursuit of those who stray, honest and restorative correction, and forgiveness without limit, because each member lives by a mercy that cancelled an unpayable debt.

outline.t: Greatness in the kingdom is measured by taking the low place, and welcoming the least is welcoming Jesus himself.
Causing a vulnerable believer to fall is so grave that radical self-examination is better than harming another or oneself.
No member is too small to matter: the Father attends to the least, and the church must go after the one who wanders.
Sin between believers is faced, not ignored or gossiped about, beginning privately and aiming always to win the brother back.
Christ is present with his gathered people and stands behind their faithful decisions and prayers.
Forgiveness is not a ration to be counted; Lamech's endless revenge is answered by endless mercy.
God's mercy cancels a debt beyond any possibility of repayment, moved by compassion rather than by the debtor's promises.
A forgiven person who refuses mercy shows that he has not grasped what he received, and the Father takes that refusal with utmost seriousness.

teach.pitfalls:
Verses 15 to 17 are often used as a rigid procedure for every conflict, including disagreements about church policy or complaints about leaders, and sometimes as a tool to silence anyone who raises a concern publicly (‘you didn't go to him first’). The text addresses a brother's sin, often a sin against the one who goes, between members of the same community; it assumes rough equality between the two, and its aim is to win the brother, not to protect reputations. It does not govern crimes, which belong to civil authorities, and it does not require a victim to confront an abuser alone. Verse 17, ‘regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector’, is sometimes taken as license for shunning or contempt; Matthew's readers knew that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sought them, so the phrase marks a changed relationship to someone who must now be won again, not a license for cruelty.

Verses 19 and 20 are frequently quoted as a promise that any request two people agree on will be granted, or as an assurance that Jesus is present at small prayer meetings. In context they concern the community's decisions in cases of discipline; Jesus is present with his gathered people in that setting and in all their gatherings, but the verse is not a technique for getting answers to prayer. Verses 8 and 9 must never be taught in a way that could be heard as encouraging self-harm; they are hyperbole about the seriousness of sin. Verse 10 should not be pressed into detailed speculation about personal angels at the expense of its point, the worth of the least believer. Finally, the parable is not a picture of God as a cruel king, nor a sum for calculating how much forgiveness is required; its details serve its contrast between a mercy that is limitless and a heart that will not pass it on.
teach.pastoral:
This chapter must be taught with the victims of abuse in mind, because it has been used against them. Church leaders have told survivors that Matthew 18 requires them to go privately to the one who harmed them, to keep the matter inside the church, or to forgive and restore the abuser at once. None of this follows from the text. The chapter opens with the most severe warning in the Gospels against anyone who causes a little one to stumble (verse 6), and the vulnerable are the ones it protects. Abuse and other crimes should be reported to civil authorities, whom God has given to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:3-4), and in many places the law requires it. A victim is never obligated to meet an abuser alone. Forgiveness, which releases the desire for revenge and hands judgment to God, is not the same as reconciliation or restored trust, which require repentance and evidence of change (compare Luke 17:3, ‘if he repents, forgive him’), and it does not remove the need for safety or for consequences. Diane Langberg (Redeeming Power, 2020) describes how appeals to unity and forgiveness have been used to protect the powerful in churches. People who have been harmed may need time before they can forgive, and a teacher should say so.

The chapter will also press on people who have been excommunicated or shunned, on parents grieving children who have wandered from faith, and on those tormented by guilt over the harm they have done. Verses 12 to 14 are good news for all three: the Father is not willing that any little one should perish. For anyone struggling with urges to self-harm, verses 8 and 9 should be explained carefully as figures of speech, and teachers should make sure a path to help is visible.

hard.q: Does God's forgiveness depend on our forgiving others, and must victims forgive those who have not repented?
hard.a:
The objection comes in two forms. The first is theological: verse 35 says the Father will treat the unforgiving as the king treated the servant, handing him over until he repays, and it echoes 6:14-15, “if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.” If forgiveness can be withdrawn for failing to forgive, it seems to depend on our performance, which would contradict the free grace the parable itself describes. The second is moral and comes sharply from Jewish readers and from many survivors of wrongdoing. Jewish tradition teaches that wrongs against a person are forgiven only when the wrongdoer seeks out the one he harmed (m. Yoma 8:9), that forgiveness is owed to one who asks sincerely (Maimonides, Laws of Repentance 2:9-10), and that no one can forgive on behalf of others; this is the question at the heart of Simon Wiesenthal's The Sunflower (1969), where many of the Jewish respondents judged that he could not have forgiven the SS man for crimes against others. A demand for limitless and unconditional forgiveness, critics say, can place an impossible burden on victims and excuse the unrepentant.

Christian responses begin with the parable's order. The king forgives first, freely and completely, before the servant does anything; his refusal to forgive shows that the mercy never reached his heart. On this reading, which Luther gave in the Large Catechism, forgiving others is not the price of God's forgiveness but the fruit and sign of it. Traditions frame the warning differently: Catholic teaching, following the Catechism's treatment of the Lord's Prayer, holds that a heart closed to others' need of mercy cannot receive God's mercy and that grace can be lost; many Reformed interpreters read the parable as exposing a person who was never truly changed; Wesleyans and others stress that a believer can fall from grace by persistent refusal. On the second objection, Christian writers such as L. Gregory Jones (Embodying Forgiveness, 1995) and Miroslav Volf (Exclusion and Embrace, 1996) distinguish forgiveness, as releasing the claim to revenge and entrusting judgment to God, from reconciliation, which requires the wrongdoer's repentance (Luke 17:3). They agree with Jewish critics that forgiveness does not deny the wrong, excuse the offender, or remove consequences, and they note that verse 15 itself requires the sin to be named. Christians disagree about whether forgiveness in the full sense can be given before repentance, and faithful readers hold both views. All agree that a person who clings to unforgiveness is in danger, and that the parable offers no cover for pressuring the wronged to pretend nothing happened.

hard.q: Does ‘tell it to the church’ authorize church discipline and excommunication, and how can that be squared with Jesus' welcome of sinners?
hard.a:
The strongest objection is that verse 17 has licensed some of the church's worst behavior: excommunication used as a political weapon, shunning that cuts people off from family and livelihood, and procedures that give leaders power over members and silence those who speak up, including victims of abuse. Critics outside the church point to these harms; critics inside it note the tension with a Jesus who ate with tax collectors and sinners (9:10-13) and ask whether ‘regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector’ fits his teaching at all. Some historical critics judge verses 15 to 18 to reflect the rules of Matthew's own community, formed after Jesus' lifetime, since the word church assumes a settled congregation. In the Reformation era Thomas Erastus argued that Scripture gives the church no power of excommunication and that punishing sin belongs to the Christian magistrate, a view Beza answered in 1590.

Christian traditions have answered in different ways. Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches practice excommunication as a medicinal penalty, meant to bring the sinner to repentance and exercised by bishops. The Reformed tradition, following Calvin (Institutes 4.12) and the Belgic Confession (1561, article 29), counts discipline among the marks of a true church, exercised by elders with the aim of restoring the sinner and protecting the flock. Anabaptists made the ban central to the church's purity (Schleitheim, 1527), and some of their heirs practice shunning, while others have softened it. Many Baptist and free churches practice congregational discipline, taking verse 17 to mean the whole assembly. Others, especially in larger state or national churches, practice little formal discipline and stress pastoral correction. Defenders of discipline point to Paul's instructions (1 Corinthians 5:1-13; 2 Corinthians 2:5-11; Galatians 6:1), which aim at restoration and command comfort for the repentant. They add that the steps begin privately to protect the person's reputation, that the goal stated in verse 15 is winning the brother, and that the phrase about tax collectors, read in Matthew, means treating the person as one outside who must be sought again. All traditions agree that discipline that ignores the vulnerable or protects the powerful contradicts the chapter's opening warning (verse 6). How formally and how often to practice it remains a matter on which faithful churches differ.

observe: What does Jesus do and say in answer to the disciples' question about who is greatest?
What are the steps Jesus gives in verses 15 to 17, and what is the stated goal of the first step?
How much did each servant owe, and how do the pleas in verses 26 and 29 compare?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus follows the warning about causing little ones to stumble with the parable of the straying sheep? How do the two belong together?
What does it mean to forgive ‘from your heart’ (verse 35)? How is forgiving different from pretending a wrong did not happen?
How should verses 15 to 17 be applied, and not applied, when one person has power over another?
apply: Where do you find yourself caring about rank or status among other Christians, and what would it look like to take the lower place?
Is there someone you have talked about rather than talked to? What would a wise and safe first step look like?
Think of the debt you have been forgiven. Is there someone whose smaller debt you are still holding against them, and what help would you need to release it?
